OffOn Stream on American doctor tests positive for Ebola in Democratic Republic of Congo outbreak The patient developed symptoms over the weekend and tested positive late Sunday. ByYouri Benadjaoud, Jack Moore, Eric M. Strauss, David Brennan, and Mary Kekatos May 18, 2026, 10:40 PM An American doctor working in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has tested positive for Ebola amid the outbreak, according to an international Christian missions organization. Dr. Peter Stafford, a medical missionary with the missions organization Serge, was exposed while treating patients at Nyankunde Hospital, the group said Monday. He sought testing "after presenting symptoms consistent with the virus," Serge said in a statement. Serge, an international Christian missions organization, confirmed today that medical missionary Dr. Peter Stafford, pictured with his wife Rebeka, has tested positive for the Bundibugyo ebolavirus variant in Bunia, Democratic Republic of Congo. Serge Stafford has served at Nyankunde Hospital with Serge since 2023, according to the organization. Two other Serge medical missionaries, including Stafford's wife, were treating patients in the region when the outbreak began and remain asymptomatic, Serge said Monday. "Our medical teams labor in some of the most demanding settings in the world, serving vulnerable communities who have limited access to healthcare," Joel Hylton, Serge's senior director of mission, said in a statement. "We are profoundly grateful for their dedication to the people of the DRC, and we deeply lament the hardship they are enduring under this current threat. Our concern extends equally to our Congolese colleagues and friends in the region who face these same risks." The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) confirmed Monday that at least one American working in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has tested positive for Ebola, but did not identify that person. Dr. Satish K. Pillai, incident manager for the CDC's Ebola response, told reporters that the individual developed symptoms over the weekend and tested positive late Sunday. Pillai added that the patient and six other high-risk contacts are being moved to Germany for care and stressed that the risk to the U.S. general public remains low. Related Ebola outbreak in Africa is 'public health emergency of international concern,' WHO says "Given the previous experience for caring for Ebola patients, coupled with the flight times being significantly shorter, this allows us to get these persons to points of care quickly," Pillai said. Pillai said the CDC has activated its Emergency Operations Center through its country offices in the DRC and in Uganda, and is deploying technical experts that have been requested from Atlanta headquarters. The CDC said earlier Monday that it is preparing to restrict entry for travelers arriving from parts of central Africa where an Ebola outbreak has been declared, in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security. Non-U.S. passport holders will face entry restrictions if they have been in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda or South Sudan in the previous 21 days. The move is being carried out under Title 42 of the Public Health Services Act, which allows the CDC director to suspend entry of individuals into the U.S. to protect public health. A staff member of the CBCA Virunga Hospital checks a visitor's temperature using a a contactless infrared thermometer, in Goma, Democratic Republic of Congo, on May 17, 2026. Jospin Mwisha/AFP via Getty Images The order will be in effect for 30 days and does not apply to U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. Popular Reads NTSB investigation underway after Amazon cargo plane crash leaves 5 dead, 5 injured 7 hours ago Mother, allegedly 'invested' in Clancy trial, charged with murdering 2-year-old child 2 days ago ‘Dancing With the Stars’ reveals new celeb cast and their pro partners Sep 2 The CDC said it is also coordinating with airlines, international partners and port-of-entry officials to identify and manage travelers with possible Ebola exposure as well as enhancing measures like contact tracing, laboratory testing capacity and hospital readiness nationwide. On Sunday, the CDC said in a statement that a "small number of Americans" are directly affected by an Ebola outbreak occurring in the Democratic Republic of Congo. "The CDC is working with other U.S. agencies to coordinate the safe withdrawal of the Americans," the CDC said. The agency did not confirm the number of people affected, the type of exposure or whether any individuals had experienced symptoms. "We don't discuss or comment on individual dispositions," Pillai said Sunday. "It is a highly dynamic situation, and at this point, what I would say is, we continue to assess, we will continue to keep you posted as we learn more." The State Department said Monday that its officials are working with the U.S. military and the CDC on "potential repatriation of affected Americans, based on assessed exposure and health needs." U.S. embassies in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Rwanda, South Sudan and Uganda have started "monitoring groups" to track developments and communicate with Americans in the impacted areas, the State Department said. An initial $13 million in foreign aid has also been mobilized for "immediate response efforts," including "supporting surveillance, laboratory capacity, risk communication, safe burials, entry and exit screening, and clinical case management," it said. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. told ABC News on Monday that his agency is "working on" the Ebola outbreak. Related Everything you need to know about Ebola On Saturday, the World Health Organization said in a statement that the Ebola outbreak in the DRC and Uganda constituted a "public health emergency of international concern." As of Sunday, there were 10 confirmed Ebola cases and 336 suspected cases in the DRC. There had been 88 suspected deaths in the DRC, as well as two confirmed cases and one confirmed death in Uganda from people who had traveled to the DRC. Ebola virus spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person and does not spread through casual contact or air. "CDC has extensive experience and expertise in responding to Ebola outbreaks," CDC acting director Dr. Jay Bhattacharya said on a call with reporters on Friday. "It is a large outbreak, and we were just informed yesterday about it." He added, "We're absolutely committed to making sure that they can get resources as they need. We have helped with other Ebola outbreaks in the past ... we have lots of hard-earned lessons. The key thing here is to know that we are absolutely involved." This is the DRC's 17th outbreak of Ebola since the disease emerged in the 1970s, according to the WHO. This strain of Ebola is caused by Bundibugyo virus, for which there are no therapeutics or vaccines, the WHO said. OffOn Stream on American doctor tests positive for Ebola in Democratic Republic of Congo outbreak The patient developed symptoms over the weekend and tested positive late Sunday. ByYouri Benadjaoud, Jack Moore, Eric M. Strauss, David Brennan, and Mary Kekatos May 18, 2026, 10:40 PM An American doctor working in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has tested positive for Ebola amid the outbreak, according to an international Christian missions organization. Dr. Peter Stafford, a medical missionary with the missions organization Serge, was exposed while treating patients at Nyankunde Hospital, the group said Monday. He sought testing "after presenting symptoms consistent with the virus," Serge said in a statement. Serge, an international Christian missions organization, confirmed today that medical missionary Dr. Peter Stafford, pictured with his wife Rebeka, has tested positive for the Bundibugyo ebolavirus variant in Bunia, Democratic Republic of Congo. Serge Stafford has served at Nyankunde Hospital with Serge since 2023, according to the organization. Two other Serge medical missionaries, including Stafford's wife, were treating patients in the region when the outbreak began and remain asymptomatic, Serge said Monday. "Our medical teams labor in some of the most demanding settings in the world, serving vulnerable communities who have limited access to healthcare," Joel Hylton, Serge's senior director of mission, said in a statement. "We are profoundly grateful for their dedication to the people of the DRC, and we deeply lament the hardship they are enduring under this current threat. Our concern extends equally to our Congolese colleagues and friends in the region who face these same risks." The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) confirmed Monday that at least one American working in the Democratic Republic of the Congo has tested positive for Ebola, but did not identify that person. Dr. Satish K. Pillai, incident manager for the CDC's Ebola response, told reporters that the individual developed symptoms over the weekend and tested positive late Sunday. Pillai added that the patient and six other high-risk contacts are being moved to Germany for care and stressed that the risk to the U.S. general public remains low. Related Ebola outbreak in Africa is 'public health emergency of international concern,' WHO says "Given the previous experience for caring for Ebola patients, coupled with the flight times being significantly shorter, this allows us to get these persons to points of care quickly," Pillai said. Pillai said the CDC has activated its Emergency Operations Center through its country offices in the DRC and in Uganda, and is deploying technical experts that have been requested from Atlanta headquarters. The CDC said earlier Monday that it is preparing to restrict entry for travelers arriving from parts of central Africa where an Ebola outbreak has been declared, in coordination with the Department of Homeland Security. Non-U.S. passport holders will face entry restrictions if they have been in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, Uganda or South Sudan in the previous 21 days. The move is being carried out under Title 42 of the Public Health Services Act, which allows the CDC director to suspend entry of individuals into the U.S. to protect public health. A staff member of the CBCA Virunga Hospital checks a visitor's temperature using a a contactless infrared thermometer, in Goma, Democratic Republic of Congo, on May 17, 2026. Jospin Mwisha/AFP via Getty Images The order will be in effect for 30 days and does not apply to U.S. citizens or lawful permanent residents. Popular Reads NTSB investigation underway after Amazon cargo plane crash leaves 5 dead, 5 injured 7 hours ago Mother, allegedly 'invested' in Clancy trial, charged with murdering 2-year-old child 2 days ago ‘Dancing With the Stars’ reveals new celeb cast and their pro partners Sep 2 The CDC said it is also coordinating with airlines, international partners and port-of-entry officials to identify and manage travelers with possible Ebola exposure as well as enhancing measures like contact tracing, laboratory testing capacity and hospital readiness nationwide. On Sunday, the CDC said in a statement that a "small number of Americans" are directly affected by an Ebola outbreak occurring in the Democratic Republic of Congo. "The CDC is working with other U.S. agencies to coordinate the safe withdrawal of the Americans," the CDC said. The agency did not confirm the number of people affected, the type of exposure or whether any individuals had experienced symptoms. "We don't discuss or comment on individual dispositions," Pillai said Sunday. "It is a highly dynamic situation, and at this point, what I would say is, we continue to assess, we will continue to keep you posted as we learn more." The State Department said Monday that its officials are working with the U.S. military and the CDC on "potential repatriation of affected Americans, based on assessed exposure and health needs." U.S. embassies in the Democratic Republic of Congo, Rwanda, South Sudan and Uganda have started "monitoring groups" to track developments and communicate with Americans in the impacted areas, the State Department said. An initial $13 million in foreign aid has also been mobilized for "immediate response efforts," including "supporting surveillance, laboratory capacity, risk communication, safe burials, entry and exit screening, and clinical case management," it said. Health Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. told ABC News on Monday that his agency is "working on" the Ebola outbreak. Related Everything you need to know about Ebola On Saturday, the World Health Organization said in a statement that the Ebola outbreak in the DRC and Uganda constituted a "public health emergency of international concern." As of Sunday, there were 10 confirmed Ebola cases and 336 suspected cases in the DRC. There had been 88 suspected deaths in the DRC, as well as two confirmed cases and one confirmed death in Uganda from people who had traveled to the DRC. Ebola virus spreads through direct contact with the bodily fluids of an infected person and does not spread through casual contact or air. "CDC has extensive experience and expertise in responding to Ebola outbreaks," CDC acting director Dr. Jay Bhattacharya said on a call with reporters on Friday. "It is a large outbreak, and we were just informed yesterday about it." He added, "We're absolutely committed to making sure that they can get resources as they need. We have helped with other Ebola outbreaks in the past ... we have lots of hard-earned lessons. The key thing here is to know that we are absolutely involved." This is the DRC's 17th outbreak of Ebola since the disease emerged in the 1970s, according to the WHO. This strain of Ebola is caused by Bundibugyo virus, for which there are no therapeutics or vaccines, the WHO said. The WHO has declared international public health emergencies over previous Ebola outbreaks, as well as COVID-19 and mpox. That's why safe and dignified burials are critical for keeping families and community members safe. September 3, 2026 DRC Written by Christin Runkle, Communications Consultant Photos by International Medical Corps The current Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) is the fastest spreading and the second largest ever, with almost 6,200 confirmed cases and 3,000 confirmed deaths recorded so far. With such a quickly spreading and dangerous disease, education is vital. Healthcare staff and community health workers (CHWs) are doing their best to slow the spread of the disease by raising awareness of symptoms, combatting rumors and misinformation, and encouraging practices such as social distancing, handwashing and reporting suspicious cases. One of the surest ways to slow the spread of Ebola is by conducting safe and dignified burials of deceased Ebola victims. Though it might seem counterintuitive, the virus continues to be extremely active and contagious in the body, even after death, and anyone who comes into contact with the body is at high risk of contracting the virus. In fact, WHO staff who worked in Sierra Leone during the 2014 Ebola outbreak estimated that as many as 80% of cases could be linked to unsafe burial and funeral practices. Though we did do this work in Sierra Leone in 2014, our Water, Sanitation and Hygiene (WASH) team is not directly conducting safe and dignified burials in the DRC—the Red Cross and local government are handling burials during this outbreak. However, our WASH team is involved in preparing bodies for the morgue because of the dangers inherent in handling a body that contains the Ebola virus. How It Works After an Ebola patient dies in an Ebola treatment center (ETC), the WASH team decontaminates the body and the entire area around it with a 0.5% chlorine solution. They place absorbent pads with a 0.5% chlorine solution inside of the body bag so that bodily fluids won’t leak out. There are many things to consider during the preparation of the body of a person who has died from Ebola. The team tries to be sensitive to the person’s religious and traditional practices and include them whenever possible. However, they must adhere to Ebola safety protocols. For instance, loved ones are allowed to participate in any traditions that don’t involve touching or being near the body of their relative. When a Muslim passes away, for example, his or her body must be purified in a ritual called ghusl. Because non-Muslims are not permitted to partake in this ritual cleansing, only WASH team members who are Muslim (and of the same gender) are permitted to manipulate the body. Another example is when Christians want a pastor to lead mourners in prayer and singing before a burial. Gatherings like this can be allowed, but health workers encourage mourners to keep such services small and to socially distance, to prevent the spread of Ebola. After cleansing and other burial preparations are finished, our WASH team members transfer the body to a table in the morgue, decontaminating their own bodies and hands at every step. A plexiglass barrier enables loved ones to safely view the body—even with the top of the bag unzipped to show the face—without fear of contracting the virus. Meanwhile, some WASH team members travel to the burial site to ensure that the grave is dug, and that the area is decontaminated to prevent community transmission. During a training session in Guinea-Bissau in 2015, a trainer explains how to properly prepare a body as part of a safe and dignified burial. “If the community is not prepared and community engagement is not done properly, you will have resistance,” says Global WASH Advisor Theodore Sie Scott. Ebola burial teams have been attacked in cemeteries when community members haven’t understood or been adequately included in the funeral process. Accurate Information Is Key This is an area where the role of CHWs is vitally important. Our CHWs talk to members of the community about many issues surrounding Ebola—including the importance of allowing loved ones to be buried in a safe but dignified manner. This is especially important because fears and misinformation surrounding ETCs—which CHWs are also working to combat—have led many people who develop Ebola to not seek medical care. Because of this, more than two-thirds of Ebola deaths have occurred at home. After a five-day training program, participants practice what they have learned about safe and dignified burials in Guinea-Bissau in 2015. “Deaths that occur at the community level are not being handled safely,” Scott explains. However, since CHWs have started to engage with communities, people have begun to report at-home deaths. In response to these reports, the WASH team has set up outreach teams that deploy with psychosocial and health promotion teams to conduct community engagement and risk management before a body is taken from a house to the ETC where it can safely be prepared for burial. Even as the outbreak grows, there are signs of hope. “With time and with the proper community engagement messaging, things are changing,” Scott says. analysis_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 暴发 已导致近 6,200 例确诊病例和 3,000 例确诊死亡。由于病毒的活性和传染性,即使在死后也具有传染性,传播 的风险很高,不安全的埋葬方式是该疾病传播的一个重要因素。
analysis_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 国际医疗队参与提高认识和推广安全做法,但红十字会和当地政府正在直接处理埋葬事宜。应对工作正在进行中,情况正在积极调查和管理中。

news.wechat_summary_zh: 时间：目前刚果民主共和国(DRC)的埃博拉病毒暴发是传播速度最快、规模第二大的，截至目前已记录近6，200例确诊病例和3，000例死亡...；地点与对象：刚果民主共和国 (DRC) 是 暴发 的所在地。受影响的人群包括刚果民主共和国的家庭和社区成员，他们有通过不安全的埋葬方式感染病毒的风险。；事件：文章报道了刚果民主共和国目前的埃博拉病毒 暴发，强调安全和有尊严的埋葬对于防止进一步传播的重要性。该事件已确认为持续的 暴发，并正在实施具体措施。；影响与风险：暴发 已导致近 6，200 例确诊病例和 3，000 例确诊死亡。由于病毒的活性和传染性，即使在死后也具有传染性，传播 的风险很高，不安全的埋葬方式是该疾病传播的一个重要因素。；应对与不确定性：国际医疗队参与提高认识和推广安全做法，但红十字会和当地政府正在直接处理埋葬事宜。应对工作正在进行中，情况正在积极调查和管理中。
